questions.stem: Within 24 hours, four clients and two staff members on a long-term care unit develop sudden vomiting and watery diarrhea. Norovirus is suspected. Which measure is most effective in stopping the spread?

options.text: Contact precautions, soap-and-water handwashing and bleach-based cleaning
Contact precautions, with alcohol hand rub used after leaving each room
Droplet precautions for the residents who are vomiting
Cohorting ill residents together while keeping the usual cleaning products

rationale.correct: Norovirus: contact precautions, soap-and-water handwashing, bleach-based cleaning, and keeping ill staff home until 48 hours after symptoms end.

perOption.a: Norovirus resists alcohol and many disinfectants; soap and water plus a bleach-based product are recommended.
perOption.b: Alcohol rub is less effective against norovirus than handwashing with soap and water.
perOption.c: Masks protect against splashes, but the main routes are hands and surfaces.
perOption.d: Cohorting helps, but routine products may not kill norovirus.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is assigning rooms and isolation signs for five new admissions arriving from the emergency department this evening, each with a confirmed diagnosis. For each condition, choose the precautions needed in addition to standard precautions.

rationale.correct: Know the precautions for common conditions: varicella is airborne plus contact; mumps and rubella are droplet; resistant organisms and lice are contact.

perOption.r1:c1: Contact alone is not enough; varicella is airborne.
perOption.r1:c2: Varicella spreads through the air, not only droplets.
perOption.r1:c3: Varicella needs airborne and contact precautions until the lesions crust.
perOption.r2:c1: Mumps is spread by respiratory droplets.
perOption.r3:c1: CRE spreads by contact with the client and surroundings.
perOption.r3:c2: CRE is not spread by droplets.
perOption.r4:c2: Lice are not spread by droplets.
perOption.r5:c2: Use droplet precautions; pregnant staff who are not immune should not care for the client.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse who is 14 weeks pregnant is assigned to a client admitted with fever, a fine pink rash and swollen lymph nodes behind the ears. Rubella is suspected. The nurse's rubella immunity status is not on file. What should the charge nurse do?

options.text: Keep the assignment if the nurse wears a fit-tested N95 respirator
Reassign the client to a nurse who is not pregnant and is immune
Draw a rubella titer and keep the assignment while waiting for the result
Place the client on contact precautions and keep the assignment

rationale.correct: Pregnant staff who may not be immune should not care for clients with rubella or varicella.

perOption.a: A respirator lowers the risk, but a nonimmune pregnant nurse should not be exposed to rubella.
perOption.b: Rubella in pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome; exposure is avoided altogether.
perOption.c: The exposure would happen before the result is known.
perOption.d: Rubella needs droplet precautions, and the assignment is still unsafe.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client on airborne precautions for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis needs a CT scan of the chest today. The first sputum smear is pending. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client for the trip to radiology
Place an N95 respirator on the client for the trip to radiology
Have the transporter wear an N95 and leave the client unmasked
Postpone the CT scan until three sputum smears are negative

rationale.correct: Clients on airborne precautions wear a surgical mask whenever they leave the room.

perOption.a: A surgical mask on the client traps droplet nuclei at the source during transport.
perOption.b: Respirators protect the wearer; the client wears a surgical mask.
perOption.c: An unmasked client exposes everyone along the route.
perOption.d: Necessary tests can go ahead with precautions.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Transport a client on airborne precautions.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing a room for a client with suspected measles who is arriving from the emergency department. What should the nurse confirm before the client is moved into the room?

options.text: The room has negative pressure and the door will stay closed
The room has positive pressure with HEPA-filtered air
The room is near the station so the door can stay open
The window can be opened to bring in fresh outdoor air

rationale.correct: Airborne isolation rooms need verified negative pressure, a closed door and frequent air exchanges.

perOption.a: Negative pressure keeps contaminated air from flowing into the hallway.
perOption.b: Positive pressure is for protective environments and would push air out of the room.
perOption.c: An open door breaks the pressure difference.
perOption.d: An open window does not create safe, directed airflow.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The hospital has one positive-pressure (protective environment) room available, and four clients on the waiting list each need a private room. Which client should the nurse recommend for this room?

options.text: A client with active pulmonary tuberculosis on the first day of treatment
A client 7 days after an allogeneic stem cell transplant for leukemia
A client on chemotherapy with an ANC of 1,200/mm3
A client with MRSA pneumonia on IV vancomycin

rationale.correct: Protective environments (positive pressure, HEPA filtration) are for allogeneic stem cell transplant clients.

perOption.a: Tuberculosis needs negative pressure so air does not leave the room.
perOption.b: Severely immunocompromised clients need protection from outside organisms.
perOption.c: This neutrophil count is only mildly low and does not need a protective environment.
perOption.d: MRSA needs contact precautions, and positive pressure would push organisms outward.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's daughter arrives to visit her father, who is on contact precautions for a VRE wound infection. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell her visits are not allowed while he is on contact precautions
Teach her hand hygiene and the visitor PPE policy
Let her enter without precautions, as she is family
Ask the client to meet her in the lobby instead

rationale.correct: Teach visitors about precautions and hand hygiene.

perOption.a: Visitors are usually allowed with precautions.
perOption.b: Visitors follow precautions according to facility policy.
perOption.c: Visitors can carry organisms to others.
perOption.d: The client should not leave the room unnecessarily.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The antimicrobial stewardship team is teaching nurses on a medical unit. Which actions support antimicrobial stewardship? Select all that apply.

options.text: Collecting cultures before the first antibiotic dose
Prompting a review of antibiotics at 48 to 72 hours
Using the shortest effective course for the infection
Teaching clients not to share or save antibiotics
Asking for an antibiotic for a client with a cold
Keeping clients on IV antibiotics until discharge

rationale.correct: Stewardship means the right drug, at the right dose, for the right duration, only when needed.

perOption.a: Cultures guide narrowing to the right drug.
perOption.b: The review allows de-escalation or stopping.
perOption.c: Shorter effective courses reduce resistance and side effects.
perOption.d: This reduces misuse.
perOption.f: Switching to oral therapy when appropriate is part of stewardship.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse has just drawn blood from a client using a safety needle. The sharps container is across the room. What should the nurse do with the needle?

options.text: Activate the safety device, then carry it to the sharps container
Recap it with two hands so it can be carried safely across the room
Bend the needle against the tray so it cannot be reused
Leave it on the bedside table and dispose of it after labeling

rationale.correct: Never recap with two hands; activate safety devices and dispose of sharps right away.

perOption.a: Activating the safety feature at once, then disposing of it, prevents needlestick injuries.
perOption.b: Two-handed recapping is a common cause of needlesticks.
perOption.c: Bending needles causes injuries.
perOption.d: An uncovered needle left out is a hazard to the nurse and others.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is changing the bed of a client who was incontinent of stool. How should the nurse handle the soiled linen?

options.text: Hold it close to the body while carrying it out
Roll it inward and hold it away from the body
Shake it out first to check for belongings
Put it on the floor until the bed is made

rationale.correct: Handle linen with minimal agitation, rolled inward and away from the body.

perOption.a: This contaminates the uniform.
perOption.b: This contains contamination.
perOption.c: Shaking spreads organisms.
perOption.d: This contaminates the environment.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is about to insert an indwelling urinary catheter and must put on sterile gloves using the open method. Place the steps in order, from first to last.

items.text: Pull the second glove on and adjust both gloves, touching only sterile surfaces
Pick up the first glove by the folded cuff with the nondominant hand
Slide the dominant hand into the first glove
Perform hand hygiene and open the glove package on a clean, dry surface
Slide the gloved fingers under the cuff of the second glove

rationale.correct: Sterile gloving: bare skin touches only the inside of the cuff, and sterile touches only sterile.

perOption.a: This prepares a sterile field.
perOption.b: Only the inside of the cuff is touched with bare skin.
perOption.c: This keeps the outside of the glove sterile.
perOption.d: Sterile touches sterile.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a sterile central line dressing change, the nurse's gloved hand brushes the bed rail while reaching for the antiseptic. The new dressing is not yet on. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue, since the bed rail was cleaned at the start of the shift
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene and put on new sterile gloves
Wipe the glove with an alcohol pad and let it dry before going on
Finish with the other hand, keeping the touched hand off the field

rationale.correct: Any break in sterile technique must be corrected before the procedure continues.

perOption.a: The glove is now contaminated, whatever the rail looked like.
perOption.b: Contaminated gloves are replaced before the procedure continues.
perOption.c: Alcohol does not make a glove sterile again.
perOption.d: The contaminated glove may still touch the field.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Correct a break in sterile technique.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for four clients. Which procedure requires surgical asepsis (sterile technique) rather than medical asepsis (clean technique)?

options.text: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
Giving a feeding through an established gastrostomy tube
Suctioning the mouth with a Yankauer catheter
Removing a peripheral IV catheter from the forearm

rationale.correct: Sterile technique is used when entering sterile body areas, such as the bladder, or caring for central lines.

perOption.a: Entering a sterile body cavity requires sterile technique.
perOption.b: The GI tract is not sterile; clean technique is used.
perOption.c: Oral suctioning uses clean technique.
perOption.d: Removing a peripheral IV uses clean technique.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with long-standing type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy reports burning pain in both feet at night and asks for a heating pad. The client cannot feel a monofilament on either sole. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply the heating pad on the low setting for 20 minutes, checking the skin after
Explain that heat can burn feet that can't feel it, and offer other relief
Wrap the heating pad in a towel and leave it on while the client sleeps
Ask the client's spouse to check the pad's temperature by hand

rationale.correct: Avoid heat therapy on areas with reduced sensation, and treat neuropathic pain with other measures and prescribed drugs.

perOption.a: Even low heat can burn skin that cannot sense temperature.
perOption.b: Loss of sensation means the client cannot feel heat damage; other measures are offered.
perOption.c: Prolonged heat on insensate skin causes burns.
perOption.d: The spouse's sense of warmth does not protect skin that cannot feel heat.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is applying a cold pack to a client's sprained ankle 1 hour after the injury. Which action is correct?

options.text: Place the ice pack directly on the skin
Cover the pack and apply it for 15 to 20 minutes
Leave the pack in place overnight
Alternate it with a heating pad every 5 minutes

rationale.correct: Cold therapy: a protective layer, 15 to 20 minutes, and a skin check.

perOption.a: Direct ice can cause frostbite.
perOption.b: A covering and a time limit prevent tissue injury.
perOption.c: Prolonged cold damages tissue.
perOption.d: Heat in the first days increases swelling.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is helping a client with right-sided weakness after a stroke move from the bed to a wheelchair for the first time. What should the nurse do before the transfer?

options.text: Lock the bed and wheelchair wheels and put on a gait belt
Place the wheelchair on the client's right, weaker side
Raise the bed to its highest position to make standing easier
Have the client put both arms around the nurse's neck

rationale.correct: Before a transfer: lock wheels, use a gait belt, and place the chair on the client's stronger side.

perOption.a: Locked wheels keep the bed and chair still, and a gait belt gives the nurse a safe hold.
perOption.b: The chair goes on the stronger (left) side so the client can pivot on the strong leg.
perOption.c: The bed should be level with the chair seat or a little higher, not at its highest.
perOption.d: This can injure the nurse and does not support the client safely.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A nurse needs to lift a heavy carton of IV fluids from the floor of the supply room onto a shelf at waist height. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Bend at the waist with straight legs and lift with the arms
Bend the knees, keep the back straight and hold the carton close
Twist the body toward the shelf while lifting the carton
Hold the carton at arm's length to keep it off the uniform

rationale.correct: Body mechanics: a wide base, bent knees, the load held close, and no twisting.

perOption.a: This strains the lower back.
perOption.b: This uses the leg muscles and keeps the load near the center of gravity.
perOption.c: Twisting while lifting increases back injury.
perOption.d: Holding a load away from the body increases strain.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: On a night round, the nurse finds a confused 88-year-old client with the head and neck wedged in the gap between the mattress and a raised half-rail. The nurse frees the client, who is unhurt. Which risk does this show, and how is it best prevented?

options.text: Entrapment and asphyxia; prevented by mattress fit and rail checks
Falls from bed; prevented by raising the rails on both sides at night
Pressure injury; prevented by turning the client every 2 hours
Wandering; prevented by a bed exit alarm and a room near the station

rationale.correct: Bed entrapment is prevented by the right mattress fit, regular bed-system checks and rail assessment.

perOption.a: Gaps between rails and mattresses cause entrapment; the bed system is checked and fitted.
perOption.b: Raising all rails can increase entrapment and fall injuries.
perOption.c: Turning prevents pressure injury, but that is not the danger shown here.
perOption.d: These help with wandering but do not remove the gap that trapped the client.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The charge nurse is doing a fall-safety round on a medical unit at 2200. Highlight the findings that need to be corrected.

cells: Bed in the lowest position with brakes locked
Call light on the floor out of the client's reach
Wet floor near the bathroom with no warning sign
Client walking in socks without grips

rationale.correct: Safety rounds find fall hazards early: call lights, floors, footwear and equipment within reach.

perOption.r2: The client cannot call for help.
perOption.r5: This is a slip hazard; non-skid footwear is needed.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client admitted for a week of IV antibiotics asks to use the hair dryer brought from home. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Let the client use it, since it belongs to the client
Have the dryer checked under facility policy before it is used
Let the client use it in the shower room where there is an outlet
Plug it into an extension cord so it reaches the bathroom mirror

rationale.correct: Personal electrical devices are checked for safety before use in the hospital.

perOption.a: Personal electrical devices may be unsafe in a hospital.
perOption.b: Biomedical engineering checks personal devices for electrical safety.
perOption.c: Using electrical devices near water is a shock hazard.
perOption.d: Extension cords add electrical hazards.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: While adjusting an IV pump, the nurse feels a mild tingling shock. The client's antibiotic is running through the pump. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep using the pump, but touch it only when wearing gloves
Replace the pump, tag it as faulty and send it for repair
Wrap the pump in a towel so the metal parts are covered
Unplug the pump, plug it back in and see if the tingling stops

rationale.correct: Remove faulty electrical equipment from service at once, tag it and report it.

perOption.a: Gloves do not prevent electrical injury from a faulty device.
perOption.b: Faulty equipment is taken out of service and repaired before reuse.
perOption.c: Covering the pump does not fix the fault.
perOption.d: This does not fix the fault and risks another shock.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Several unrelated adults arrive at the emergency department over 2 days with high fever and back pain, followed by a rash of firm, deep blisters that are all at the same stage and are thickest on the face, arms and palms. None of them has traveled recently or been vaccinated against smallpox. Which agent does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Smallpox
Chickenpox
Anthrax
Monkeypox

rationale.correct: Suspected smallpox needs airborne and contact precautions and immediate notification of public health.

perOption.a: Smallpox lesions are deep, firm, all at the same stage, and thickest on the face and limbs, including the palms.
perOption.b: Varicella lesions appear in crops at different stages and are thickest on the trunk.
perOption.c: Cutaneous anthrax causes a painless black eschar, not a widespread blistering rash.
perOption.d: Mpox lesions can look similar but usually come with swollen lymph nodes and often start in the genital area.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A respiratory virus pandemic is spreading in the region, and the hospital expects a surge of admissions. Which action by the hospital best supports safe care?

options.text: Train staff in PPE use and plan cohort units and surge capacity
Reserve N95 respirators for intensive care staff to save supplies
Pause hand hygiene audits so staff can focus on caring for clients
Admit clients to shared rooms in order of arrival, whatever the diagnosis

rationale.correct: Pandemic preparedness: PPE training, cohorting and surge planning.

perOption.a: Preparation reduces transmission and keeps care going during a surge.
perOption.b: Rationing respirators for staff exposed elsewhere puts them at risk.
perOption.c: Hand hygiene matters even more during a pandemic.
perOption.d: Mixing infected and uninfected clients increases spread.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two days after a hurricane, a nurse is working at an emergency shelter. Which person needs the nurse's attention first?

options.text: A 40-year-old with type 1 diabetes who has had no insulin for a day and is now confused
A 72-year-old with COPD whose inhaler ran out, who has mild wheezing and an SpO2 of 93%
An 8-year-old with a 3 cm laceration on the forearm that has stopped bleeding
A 30-year-old who is breathing fast and has tingling fingers after seeing the damage

rationale.correct: In shelters, see first people with chronic illness who have lost their medication and now have new, serious symptoms.

perOption.a: Missed insulin with new confusion suggests diabetic ketoacidosis or severe glucose changes, which are life-threatening.
perOption.b: This person needs a replacement inhaler soon but is stable.
perOption.c: A clean, controlled wound can wait for care.
perOption.d: Anxiety-related hyperventilation needs calm support but is not life-threatening.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A radiology technologist arrives to take a portable chest x-ray of a client the nurse is caring for. The nurse is hanging an IV bag at the bedside. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Finish hanging the IV at the bedside while the x-ray is taken
Step out of the room or stand behind a lead shield during the x-ray
Hold the client's arm out of the way during the x-ray without an apron
Ask a pregnant coworker to help position the client during the x-ray

rationale.correct: Radiation safety uses time, distance and shielding.

perOption.a: Staying close without protection increases exposure.
perOption.b: Distance and shielding reduce exposure.
perOption.c: If holding is needed, a lead apron and gloves are worn.
perOption.d: Pregnant staff should avoid radiation exposure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An old mercury thermometer that a client brought from home breaks on the floor of the room, and small beads of mercury roll under the bed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Vacuum the beads up so that no mercury is left behind
Keep people out and follow the hazardous spill procedure
Sweep the beads into a dustpan and put them in the trash
Wipe the beads up with a wet paper towel and rinse it in the sink

rationale.correct: Follow the hazardous spill procedure and keep people out of the area until it is cleaned.

perOption.a: Vacuuming spreads mercury vapor through the air.
perOption.b: Mercury is hazardous and needs special cleanup with a spill kit.
perOption.c: Mercury must not go in regular trash.
perOption.d: Rinsing mercury down the sink contaminates the water supply.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An emergency department nurse is reviewing five clients waiting for admission, each with fever and cough, some with a rash. Two private rooms with negative pressure are available, and the rest of the unit has ordinary private rooms with the doors kept closed. Select the 2 conditions that require an airborne infection isolation room.

options.text: Measles
Disseminated herpes zoster
Influenza
Pertussis
Meningococcal meningitis

rationale.correct: Airborne: measles, varicella, disseminated zoster and tuberculosis.

perOption.a: Measles is airborne.
perOption.b: Disseminated zoster needs airborne and contact precautions.
perOption.c: Influenza needs droplet precautions.
perOption.d: Pertussis needs droplet precautions.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client transferred from a long-term care facility has a skin swab positive for Candida auris colonization. The client has no signs of infection. Which action is most important?

options.text: Contact precautions and cleaning with a disinfectant that kills C. auris
Standard precautions, since the client has no signs of infection
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room until swabs are negative
An antifungal course to clear the colonization before any other care

rationale.correct: C. auris: contact precautions, a disinfectant effective against it, and notifying infection prevention.

perOption.a: C. auris spreads on hands and surfaces and resists many disinfectants and antifungals.
perOption.b: Colonized clients can spread C. auris to others.
perOption.c: C. auris is not airborne.
perOption.d: Colonization is not treated with antifungals; infection control is the priority.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A new graduate is about to irrigate a client's infected abdominal wound and asks whether eye protection is needed. Which answer by the nurse is correct?

options.text: "Wear it whenever a splash of blood or body fluid is likely."
"Wear it for clients who are known to have a bloodborne infection."
"Wear it during sterile procedures, such as inserting a catheter."
"Wear it if you can't wear gloves for the procedure."

rationale.correct: Choose PPE based on the expected exposure: eye protection for any likely splash.

perOption.a: Standard precautions include eye protection whenever a splash is likely.
perOption.b: Standard precautions apply to every client, whatever the diagnosis.
perOption.c: Eye protection depends on splash risk, not on sterility.
perOption.d: Gloves protect the hands, not the eyes.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
